translation:
Guru Gopaldasji, the guru of Jivanji, lived at this place. Nothing has remained after him that would serve as a memorial, so this Chorenda is regarded as a place of merit (punya sthali) simply because it was Guru Gopaldasji's residence.

The writing on pages 95 to 97 of handwritten manuscript no. 28 was copied by the revered Yadunath into pages 340–345 of handwritten manuscript no. 111. It was printed in Jivanvani, Year 1, Issue 2, on the full-moon day of Falgun, Samvat 2032, pages 1–2, and reads as follows. It mentions Chorenda and records an episode from the life of Jivanji.

Ramkabir: _Jivanji Maharaj Dhanore padharya te Chanderiyethi Chorande padharya._ (Jivanji Maharaj arrived at Dhanora, having come to Chorenda from Chanderiya.)

Jivandasji arrived at Dhanora together with Gopaldasji, Santdasji, and Rupa Bhagat. Devdasji and Gopaldasji had arrived at Dhanora, coming by way of Deva Sahi from Chanderiya to Chorenda. On the occasion of the Sharad-nisha festival (the autumn full-moon night celebration), they came, on the way, to a village named Dhanora, where Jivandasji and the other Vaishnavs all sat beneath a peepal tree by the lake, and hari-kirtan (devotional singing) was taking place. Now this peepal tree was dry, withered away. The village Patels (headmen) sent a man to cut it down, but Jivandasji said, "The peepal tree is in fact green — it must not be cut. Moreover, the peepal tree is spoken of in the Gita too, that it is not to be cut." This is the word of the Gita, chapter 10:

_Ashvattha sarvavrikshanam devarshinam cha Naradah, Gandharvanam Chitrarathah siddhanam Kapilo munih. ||25||_ (Among trees I am the peepal; among the divine sages, Narada; among the Gandharvas, Chitratha; among the perfected beings, the sage Kapila — Bhagavad Gita 10.25.)

Note: Trees speak, and they plead too; the example of the peepal tree fits this account well. (Kalyan, Year 33, Issue 9, page 1201.)

_Hari daal mat todiye, laage sukha baan, das Maluka yon kahe, apni so 'jiya jaan'._ (Do not cut a green branch — it feels as if struck by a dry arrow; so says servant Maluka: know it as you would know your own [pain].) (Jagdish's manuscript no. 258; Shamal Haribhai's no. 1, part 1, page 141.)

Then that man went back and reported that the peepal had indeed turned green. Hearing this, all the villagers came and had darshan of the saints. As they did so their minds grew clear, and they asked, "This peepal was dry — how did it turn green?" Jivandasji said, "This peepal dried up on account of the bones of an ungrateful person, and that is also why water does not stay in the lake."

_Kritaghni ke haadsu peepal suko jaay, kunvarika ku doshan lagyo, kahi samjhavi chinh._ (Because of the bones of an ungrateful one the peepal withers; blame fell upon a maiden — so it is told and explained.) (Najarnani's no. 8, page 32.)

Note: See Amarcharitra, part 5, pages 245–247. Registration no. 251/15, "Janabai, the Image of Devotion."

_So jivan lilo kiyo, satguru tane pasaay._ (Thus Jivan[dasji] made it green, by the grace of the true guru.)

Then it became known that he was some great and holy soul. Knowing this, they came with a request and said, "In our family there is a girl who has been disabled in body since birth." They brought her and placed her at his feet in surrender. He then said to Santdasji, "Go, fill water from the lake." Santdasji took the kamandal (water pot) and went, but no water came, so he returned and told the Maharaj there was no water. Jivandasji said, "Brothers, in this world the peepal has dried up on account of the bones of an ungrateful man, and there is also no water in the lake — but by the power of the saints, water will come." He then sent Santdas again, saying, "Go — there is water in the lake now."

_Adhik badhavat aapte, jan mahima Raghuvir, savari pad raj prasatan, sudh bhayo salita nir. ||1||_ (The glory of the Lord's devotee grows ever greater, like [that of] Raghuvir [Lord Ram]; through the touch of the dust of his feet [as with Shabari], the water of the river became pure. (1)) (Najar's large notebook no. 9, page 46; Venkateshwar Press, Bhaktavala, page 27.)

In this way water appeared. Santdasji brought the water and gave it to the Maharaj, who took it and sprinkled it on the girl's body and had her drink it; her disability left her body, she became radiant, and knowledge (gyan) dawned within her.

The words of Harmabai: _Harmabai harakhiyan Jivan darshan paay, sarid sanso mitiyo, bhayo gyan prakash._ (Harmabai rejoiced on receiving the darshan of Jivan[dasji]; all doubt and distress were dispelled, and the light of knowledge dawned.)

The words of Harmabai: _Gyan prakashi guru miliya, so kem visaryo jaay, jo Govind kripa kare, guru malege aay._ (The guru who kindled the light of knowledge — how could he ever be forgotten? If Govind [the Lord] shows grace, the guru will come and be met again.)

Reckon these as her sakhis of joy. They rejoiced, saying that this girl was some blessed, divine being. Recognizing this, Jivandasji placed his hand upon her head. Hearing of this happening, Ratansinghji said, "I offer this girl to you; please accept her." Hearing this, Jivandasji replied, "We have set out to wander through the land, and ours is the life of a sadhu (mendicant), so this is not fitting for us." Then, pleading earnestly, Harmabai said:

_Tumku chhod avar kyan jaau, nisdin tumari sang rahavun._ (Leaving you, where else could I go? Day and night I would remain in your company.)

Hearing these words of Harmabai, he accepted her — just as, of old, Lord Jagannath Swami gave Padmavati to the devotee Jaidevji, so too did Jivandasji, by Hari's will, accept Harmabai. He himself stayed there for one month, performed hari-kirtan, and gave everyone the teaching of knowledge (gyan). He then told Harmabai, "We shall go visit Jagannathji, Naimisharanya, Kashi, Ayodhya, Mathura, and Badrikashram; when we return we shall look after you." Saying this, he set out for Chorenda.

This account was copied out of devotion from the notebook of the Vaishnav Dana Bhagat of Malwa and Savji Bhagat, by Bhagat Kashiram, a resident of Bhoj village, and I include it here through the tradition of the saints. (Handwritten manuscript no. 25, page 97.) The Malwa notebook was copied out in the month of Magha, Samvat 1836. See handwritten manuscript no. 111, pages 346–347.
